def: A membrane-bound vesicle formed when a phagocyte engulfs a particle or microbe. It fuses with a lysosome to form a phagolysosome, where the contents are degraded.
A genus of filamentous actinomycete bacteria. S. rectivirgula grows in moldy hay and causes farmer's lung, a hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
A hypersensitivity pneumonitis from inhaling avian proteins in droppings or feathers, seen in pigeon breeders. Causes cough and dyspnea from type III and IV reactions.
Gram-positive, branching filamentous bacteria that form hyphae-like growth, such as Actinomyces, Nocardia and Streptomyces. Many live in soil and moldy hay.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from inhaling spores of thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay. Immune complexes and T cells cause cough, dyspnea and, if chronic, pulmonary fibrosis.
Inflammation of the spinal cord, often causing weakness, sensory loss and bladder dysfunction below the level of the lesion.
Inflammation across one level of the spinal cord that causes bilateral weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction. Associated with viral infection, multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica.
A precancerous glandular lesion of cells that look malignant but have not invaded beyond the basement membrane. Seen in the cervix and as a precursor of lung adenocarcinoma.
A fracture through bone weakened by disease, such as metastasis, osteoporosis or Paget disease, occurring with minimal or no trauma.
The highest sympathetic ganglion in the neck. Its postganglionic fibers supply the pupillary dilator and sweat glands of the face; interruption causes Horner syndrome.
A selective COX-2 inhibitor NSAID that spares COX-1 and so causes less GI bleeding. Contains a sulfonamide group; raises cardiovascular risk.

Coagulation factor at the start of the common pathway, activated by both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. Activated factor Xa converts prothrombin to thrombin; inhibited by heparin and direct Xa inhibitors.
A serine protease that converts plasminogen to plasmin, which dissolves fibrin clots. Alteplase is the drug, used for acute ischemic stroke, MI and pulmonary embolism; bleeding is the main risk.
The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; inhibited by ATP and citrate.
Precipitates of denatured hemoglobin inside red cells, seen with supravital stain. Found in G6PD deficiency and alpha thalassemia; their removal by splenic macrophages produces bite cells.
A small heme protein in the mitochondrial intermembrane space that shuttles electrons between complexes III and IV. Its release into the cytosol triggers apoptosis.
A mitochondrial uncoupler that carries protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient so oxygen use continues without ATP synthesis, producing heat. Toxic cause of hyperthermia.
The liver enzyme that removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate, releasing free glucose in gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Deficient in von Gierke disease.
Autosomal recessive periodic fever syndrome from MEFV (pyrin) mutations, causing episodes of fever with serositis (abdominal pain, pleuritis). Complicated by AA amyloidosis; treated with colchicine.

Glycogen storage disease type III from deficient debranching enzyme, causing hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia and muscle weakness. Gluconeogenesis is intact, so lactate and blood glucose after fasting are variable.
Gas bubbles entering the circulation, such as via central venous catheters or lung barotrauma, and blocking vessels. Causes acute dyspnea, hypotension and neurologic deficits.
Death of lung tissue distal to a blocked pulmonary artery branch, usually from embolism. Appears as a wedge-shaped pleural-based hemorrhagic area and causes pleuritic pain and hemoptysis.
A regular heart rate above 100 beats per minute with normal P waves, originating from the sinoatrial node. A physiologic response to fever, pain, anemia or hypovolemia.
An inhaled or oral corticosteroid with high first-pass metabolism. Used for asthma, Crohn disease and eosinophilic esophagitis.
A long-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonist (anticholinergic) used for COPD and asthma. Blocks M3 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle; side effects include dry mouth.
Specialized epithelial cells with foot processes that cover the outer glomerular capillary basement membrane. They form filtration slits, and their effacement causes nephrotic syndrome.
Transporter in the distal convoluted tubule that reabsorbs Na+ and Cl- from urine; inhibited by thiazide diuretics. Inactivating mutations cause Gitelman syndrome.
Congenital malformation in which a kidney is replaced by non-functional cysts of varying size. Usually unilateral and diagnosed on ultrasound; the cause is abnormal ureteric bud development.
Deletion of 11p13 (including WT1 and PAX6) causing Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies and Intellectual disability (formerly mental Retardation).
Vaccines against Streptococcus pneumoniae. The conjugate vaccine (PCV) elicits T-cell-dependent memory in children; the polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) is used in older adults.
The most abundant antibody isotype in serum. It crosses the placenta, fixes complement, opsonizes pathogens and is the main secondary response antibody.
A monoclonal antibody against PD-1 that releases T-cell inhibition against tumors. Used for melanoma, lung cancer and others; causes immune-related adverse events such as colitis.
Extracellular deposits of amyloid beta peptide in brain tissue, with neuritic plaques surrounded by dystrophic neurites. A hallmark of Alzheimer disease.
Autosomal recessive defect of the renal transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine (COLA), causing recurrent hexagonal cystine kidney stones.
A state of near-unconsciousness in which a person can be roused only by vigorous or painful stimuli and lapses back when stimulation stops.
A device placed in the vagina to support pelvic organs in prolapse or incompetent cervix.
Rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, converting acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. Needs biotin and ATP; activated by insulin and citrate, inhibited by glucagon and AMPK.
A negatively charged nine-carbon sugar at the ends of glycoprotein and glycolipid chains. Gives cell surfaces their charge; N-acetylneuraminic acid is the main form.
Lysosomal storage disease from arylsulfatase A deficiency, causing buildup of sulfatides and CNS and peripheral demyelination with ataxia, dementia and neuropathy.

Autosomal recessive deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, causing buildup of leucine, isoleucine and valine. Causes sweet-smelling urine, poor feeding and neurologic damage; thiamine may help.
Inflammation of the tongue making it smooth, red and sore. Seen in iron, B12, folate and riboflavin deficiency.
Autosomal recessive defect of neutral amino acid transport in the intestine and kidney, causing tryptophan loss and pellagra-like rash, ataxia and dementia from niacin deficiency.
Autosomal recessive defect of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, preventing chylomicron and VLDL assembly. Causes fat malabsorption, acanthocytes, ataxia and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
A reversible VMAT2 inhibitor that depletes presynaptic dopamine. Used for chorea in Huntington disease and tardive dyskinesia; can cause depression.
A CNS stimulant that blocks dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake. First-line treatment for ADHD; may reduce appetite and cause insomnia.
A hookworm acquired by skin penetration of larvae from soil. Adult worms attach to intestinal mucosa causing iron deficiency anemia.
A hookworm genus; A. duodenale is acquired by ingestion or skin penetration and causes iron deficiency anemia through intestinal blood loss.
The genus of hookworm Necator americanus, which burrows through the skin, and causes iron deficiency anemia by intestinal blood loss.
Test that separates hemoglobin types by charge to diagnose hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease (HbS), HbC and thalassemias.
Congenital pure red cell aplasia from ribosomal protein gene mutations, presenting in infancy with macrocytic anemia, low reticulocytes and physical anomalies such as thumb abnormalities.
Clusters of pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies beside the spinal cord. Their axons carry sensory input from the periphery to the dorsal horn.
A stretch receptor within skeletal muscle with intrafusal fibers. It senses muscle length and rate of change, and mediates the stretch (myotatic) reflex.
Nerve from C5-C7 (lateral cord) supplying the biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis, then becoming the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. Injury weakens elbow flexion.
All-trans retinoic acid, a vitamin A derivative. Induces differentiation of promyelocytes in acute promyelocytic leukemia (t(15;17)); also used topically for acne. Teratogenic.
The midline part of the cerebellum controlling trunk and proximal muscles and balance. Damage (e.g., from medulloblastoma) causes truncal ataxia.
Bone marrow precursors that give rise to red cells, platelets, granulocytes and monocytes, as opposed to lymphoid progenitors.
An aggressive leukemia/lymphoma of immature T cells (TdT positive, CD3 positive). Often in adolescent males with a mediastinal mass.
Episodes of severe, brief, stabbing facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, triggered by touch or chewing. Treated with carbamazepine.
A retrovirus causing adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and tropical spastic paraparesis. Spread via breastfeeding, blood and sex; endemic in Japan and the Caribbean.
A cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with skin patches, plaques and tumors, in which CD4 T cells with cerebriform nuclei (Sezary cells) infiltrate the epidermis forming Pautrier microabscesses.
Pontine nucleus of cranial nerve VI that controls the lateral rectus. Its lesion causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy because it also contains interneurons to the opposite medial rectus.
Folded brainstem nucleus in the medulla that sends climbing fibers to the cerebellum. Hypertrophic degeneration can follow brainstem lesions.
Brainstem nuclei at the pontomedullary junction where auditory nerve fibers first synapse, then project to the superior olivary complex.
The part of the temporal bone behind the ear containing air cells that connect to the middle ear. Infection spreads to cause mastoiditis.
The cochlear membrane that vibrates with sound, carrying the organ of Corti. Its base is narrow and stiff (high frequencies) and apex wide and floppy (low frequencies).
Network of brainstem neurons in the pons that helps control sleep-wake cycles, REM sleep, and horizontal gaze (paramedian pontine reticular formation).
Artery formed by union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. Supplies the pons, cerebellum and occipital lobes; occlusion can cause locked-in syndrome.
Paralysis of one side of the body, usually from a contralateral lesion in the brain or upper spinal cord, such as stroke.
A tumor of the pineal gland, most often a germ cell tumor, that can compress the tectum and cause Parinaud syndrome (upward gaze palsy) and obstructive hydrocephalus.
An unsteady, wide-based, staggering walk due to cerebellar disease (cerebellar gait) or loss of proprioception (sensory ataxia).
Hypothalamic nucleus above the optic chiasm that serves as the body's master circadian clock; receives light input from the retina and regulates melatonin.
The occipital cortex around the calcarine fissure (Brodmann area 17) that receives visual input from the lateral geniculate nucleus. Lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
Blockage of the central or a branch retinal vein, causing sudden painless vision loss with retinal hemorrhages (blood and thunder fundus) and macular edema.
A markedly elevated white cell count (above 50,000) with left shift in response to infection or inflammation. Differs from CML by high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase and no BCR-ABL.
A cell cycle regulator that, with CDK4/6, phosphorylates Rb to drive G1 to S transition. Overexpressed in mantle cell lymphoma from t(11;14).
The anterior frontal lobe responsible for executive function, judgment, planning and personality. Damage causes disinhibition and apathy.

Meningitis from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, with a basal predominance of granulomatous inflammation. CSF shows lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose; may cause cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus.
X-linked peroxisomal disorder impairing very long chain fatty acid breakdown (ABCD1 defect), causing CNS demyelination and adrenal insufficiency.
Bladder dysfunction from nerve injury, with retention or overflow incontinence (e.g., spinal injury, diabetes, multiple sclerosis).
A peptide cleaved from amyloid precursor protein by beta- and gamma-secretase. Aggregates into plaques in Alzheimer disease.
Intraneuronal aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer disease. Their spread correlates with cognitive decline.
Tauopathy causing vertical gaze palsy, postural instability with early falls, axial rigidity and dementia; poorly responsive to levodopa.
A protease from chief cell pepsinogen, activated by gastric acid. Digests proteins in the stomach.
Air in the mediastinum, from rupture of alveoli or esophageal perforation. Causes chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema; Hamman sign is crunching with heartbeat.
Where the esophagus meets the stomach, with the lower esophageal sphincter. Site of Barrett esophagus and adenocarcinoma transition.
Carcinogenic compounds formed from nitrites and amines in cured meats. Linked to gastric cancer.
Dark, velvety thickening of skin in body folds (neck, axilla). Associated with insulin resistance, obesity and sometimes gastric adenocarcinoma.
Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces with IgA deposits at dermal papillae. Associated with celiac disease; treat with dapsone and gluten-free diet.
The thin membrane lining joint cavities, secreting synovial fluid. Inflamed in rheumatoid arthritis, forming pannus.
A chimeric anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody for Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Risks include reactivation of latent tuberculosis; screen with PPD or IGRA.
Autosomal dominant syndrome of hamartomatous GI polyps with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation (lips, buccal mucosa), from STK11 mutation. Raises risk of GI and breast cancers.
The opening where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct join and drain into the second part of the duodenum, controlled by the sphincter of Oddi.
Gallbladder inflammation without stones, typically in critically ill patients from bile stasis and ischemia (burns, sepsis, prolonged TPN).
The time taken to fall asleep. Short in sleep deprivation; REM latency (time to first REM) is shortened in depression and narcolepsy.
A tricyclic antidepressant that blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake. Used for depression and enuresis; has anticholinergic and cardiotoxic effects.
A flat red-purple capillary malformation present from birth, not resolving. When on the face in the V1 distribution it suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome.
MHC class I allele linked to seronegative spondyloarthropathies: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and IBD arthritis.
Learning in which behavior is changed by its consequences: reinforcement increases and punishment decreases its frequency. Described by Skinner.
Process increasing the likelihood of a behavior. Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus; negative reinforcement removes an aversive one.
Adult pattern of disregard for others' rights, deceit and lack of remorse, beginning with conduct disorder before age 15. Diagnosed only at age 18 or older.
Coating of a pathogen with molecules such as IgG or C3b to enhance phagocytosis.
A long-acting benzodiazepine used for insomnia. Active metabolites persist, increasing risk of daytime sedation.
Fecal-oral RNA virus hepatitis, self-limited but with high mortality in pregnant women. Endemic in developing countries.
A nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic that acts at the GABA-A receptor's BZ1 site. Used for insomnia; complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking are a risk.
An ultra-short-acting barbiturate IV induction anesthetic. Rapid onset from high lipid solubility and redistribution; can cause hypotension.
A penicillinase-resistant penicillin. Its resistance gene mecA encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) in MRSA.

Neurologic symptoms (paralysis, blindness, seizures) with no medical explanation, thought to stem from psychological stress and not intentionally feigned. Also called functional neurologic symptom disorder.
An antidepressant with serotonin reuptake inhibition and receptor modulation; used for major depression.
Inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, so drinking alcohol causes a toxic buildup of acetaldehyde (flushing, nausea). Used to deter alcohol use.
The difference in event rate between control and treated groups. Its inverse is the number needed to treat.
Benign hereditary defect in canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin (MRP2) with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a black liver on biopsy.
Crystals that deposit in cartilage and cause pseudogout. Seen in joint fluid as rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals.
Severe wasting with loss of muscle and fat that is not reversed by eating, seen in advanced cancer, heart failure and AIDS. Mediated by TNF-alpha.
Rapid loss of liver function with coagulopathy and encephalopathy in a patient with no prior liver disease. Causes include acetaminophen toxicity and viral hepatitis.
A toxin from Aspergillus flavus on stored grains and nuts, a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma. It causes p53 mutations.
Self molecules that the immune system mistakenly attacks, causing autoimmune disease.
A live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis vaccine used for tuberculosis prevention in endemic areas. Makes the tuberculin skin test positive.
Tissue transplanted between genetically different members of the same species. Prone to rejection.
Cytoplasmic protein complex that activates caspase-1, which cleaves pro-IL-1beta into active IL-1beta, in response to danger signals.
Cell surface adhesion receptors that bind extracellular matrix and other cells. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 results from beta-2 integrin defects.
Infection by organisms that rarely cause disease in healthy people but affect those with weak immunity, such as in AIDS.
An antiphospholipid antibody that prolongs aPTT in vitro (not corrected by mixing) but causes thrombosis in vivo.
A growth factor that stimulates epithelial cell proliferation by binding EGFR, a receptor tyrosine kinase. EGFR is overexpressed in some lung and colorectal cancers.
The dense connective tissue membrane covering the outer surface of bones, with nerves and blood vessels and osteogenic cells.
Inflammation of a tendon and its synovial sheath, causing pain and swelling. Causes include gonococcal infection and overuse.
Autoimmune loss of melanocytes causing depigmented white patches on the skin.
Self-limited rash starting with a herald patch, followed by oval scaly lesions along skin cleavage lines in a Christmas tree pattern.
Infection with Bartonella henselae transmitted by a cat scratch, causing tender regional lymphadenopathy and fever.
A drug that lowers fever, such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs, by decreasing hypothalamic prostaglandin E2.
A double-stranded DNA virus causing warts and cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancers. High-risk types 16 and 18 produce E6 and E7, inhibiting p53 and Rb.
An extended-spectrum penicillin active against Pseudomonas, usually combined with clavulanate.
A second-generation cephalosporin active against H. influenzae, Moraxella and Klebsiella, used for respiratory tract infections.
Drugs such as anastrozole and letrozole that block estrogen synthesis from androgens, used for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
Upper abdominal discomfort, bloating or early satiety after eating; causes include ulcers, GERD and functional disease.
An oral chelating agent (DMSA) for lead poisoning in children.
Viral proteins forming the protein shell that encloses and protects viral genetic material.
Creation of an opening in the chest wall to drain air or fluid, as with a chest tube for pneumothorax or effusion.
C-shaped fibrocartilage pad in the knee between femur and tibia that absorbs shock. The medial meniscus is more often torn.
An enveloped RNA paramyxovirus that causes bronchiolitis in infants. Forms syncytia in cell culture; prevented with palivizumab in high-risk infants.
Surgical removal of plaque from an artery lining, such as carotid endarterectomy for stenosis to prevent stroke.
A dimorphic fungus (B. dermatitidis) with broad-based budding yeast, causing pulmonary and skin disease in the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys.
A dermatophyte fungus causing tinea infections of skin, hair and nails.
A topical azole antifungal that inhibits ergosterol synthesis, used for candidiasis and tinea infections.
Infection with Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus from thorn pricks of rose bushes, producing ascending nodular lymphangitis ("rose gardener's disease"). Treated with itraconazole.
An echinocandin antifungal that inhibits beta-glucan synthesis in the cell wall, used for invasive Candida and Aspergillus infections.
An azole antifungal and the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis. Inhibits ergosterol synthesis; can cause visual disturbances and hepatotoxicity.
Toxin of Shigella dysenteriae and EHEC that inactivates the 60S ribosome, causing bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
RNA viruses whose genome must be copied into mRNA by a viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase carried in the virion. Includes influenza, measles, rabies and Ebola.
The mild, Th1-driven form of leprosy with few well-demarcated anesthetic skin lesions and rare bacilli.
Intrauterine Toxoplasma gondii infection causing chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications.
An antimalarial for chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium; adverse effects include neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Fever in a patient with a low absolute neutrophil count (below 500), usually from chemotherapy. A medical emergency needing prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Tick-borne infection by Ehrlichia chaffeensis that infects monocytes, forming morulae, with fever and leukopenia.
A chemically inactivated tetanus toxin used in vaccines to induce immunity to Clostridium tetani.
Clonal proliferation of mast cells (often KIT D816V), causing flushing, itching and anaphylaxis, with tryptase elevated.
A carbapenem with broad coverage; given with cilastatin to prevent renal degradation. May cause seizures.
Disease from Bacillus anthracis spores, causing black eschar skin lesions or fatal inhalational mediastinitis. Toxins include edema factor, lethal factor and protective antigen.
A combined childhood vaccine against diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis.
A lab test that detects a substance using antibody binding, such as ELISA.
Gram-negative rod acquired from contaminated pork, causing enterocolitis, pseudoappendicitis (mesenteric lymphadenitis) and growth at cold temperatures.
Family of enveloped positive-sense RNA viruses spread by mosquitoes and ticks, including dengue, yellow fever, Zika, West Nile and hepatitis C.
Drugs ending in -navir that block cleavage of viral polyproteins to prevent maturation. Side effects include hyperglycemia and lipodystrophy.
An antimetabolite that inhibits DNA polymerase, used for acute myeloid leukemia. Toxicity includes cerebellar dysfunction.
A topoisomerase II inhibitor chemotherapy used for small cell lung cancer and testicular cancer; causes myelosuppression.
A topoisomerase II inhibitor chemotherapy used in childhood leukemia, similar to etoposide.
A genus of lung flukes acquired by eating undercooked crustaceans (crabs, crayfish).
A lung fluke acquired by eating undercooked crab or crayfish, causing chronic cough and hemoptysis resembling tuberculosis.
Larval stage of filarial worms found in the blood or skin, transmitted to humans by insect bites.
A genus of filarial nematodes causing lymphatic filariasis.
Nematode transmitted by mosquitoes, causing lymphatic filariasis with lymphedema and elephantiasis.
Massive dilation of the colon without a mechanical blockage, in hospitalized or postoperative patients. Called Ogilvie syndrome; treated with neostigmine.
Surgery wrapping the stomach fundus around the lower esophagus to treat severe GERD (e.g., Nissen).
A potent opioid agonist, stronger than morphine, used for severe pain.
The stage of viral replication in which the capsid is removed to release viral nucleic acid in the host cell.
